title: Stream offload and tool latency playbook (PRD draft)
summary: Draft PRD proposing a playbook for streaming responses that may trigger high-latency tool calls. Introduces an offload-first pattern, progressive structured frames, and SDK ergonomics to surface partial results, tool progress, and graceful degradation while keeping latency SLOs for the main response path.
body:
Context:

Redwood's hosted streaming surface increasingly sees mixes of low-latency text synthesis and higher-latency tool calls (external APIs, database lookups, search, heavy compute). Customers want predictable token-latency for user-facing interactions while still being able to leverage long-running tool resolution. Current options: block the stream until tools finish (bad UX) or return a placeholder and push a separate event (ad-hoc and inconsistent across SDKs). This PRD proposes a consistent offload and staged-output model with SDK primitives for progressive frames, tool-progress telemetry, and resume/commit semantics.

Goals (primary):
- Keep initial token latency within existing SLOs for interactive flows (p50 < 100ms where configured).
- Provide a developer-standard way to include tool-driven enrichment without blocking the primary text stream.
- Ship SDK ergonomics that make progressive frames simple to consume and robust to network interruptions.
- Make tool-level telemetry and quality signals first-class for Optimize and Console.

Goals (secondary):
- Allow customers to opt into strong consistency (blocking tool calls) per route.
- Preserve auditability for tool outputs (attribution, timestamps, signatures).

High-level approach:
1) Offload-first stream pattern: the LLM streaming channel emits an immediate progressive result (base text + metadata) while tool calls the model would logically request are queued to an internal offload pipeline. Tool results are attached to the stream later as delta frames when they complete or as separate resume events.

2) Structured progressive frames: define small typed frames that travel over the same streaming connection. Frame types include: text_delta, partial_json, tool_progress, tool_result, commit_marker, resume_token. Each frame is self-describing and machine-typed in the payload so SDKs can offer typed callbacks.

3) Toollet execution model: offloaded work runs in a prioritized queue. Work has a tier (fast/medium/slow), a fallback policy (best-effort/required), and an expiration. Fallbacks may be configured globally, per-route, or by SDK.

4) SDK ergonomics: streaming AsyncIterator plus event callbacks. Provide first-class helpers: onFrame(type, handler), awaitCommit(token), resumeFrom(token). Mobile and thin clients get a smaller surface with snapshot hooks.

API surface (proposal sketch):
- POST /v1/generate/stream (existing) accepts new options: offload_policy, frame_schema, fallback_policy
- POST /v1/streams/resume with resume_token to request late-bound frames or commit status
- Webhook/backchannel: optional callback for completed tool_result when client is offline

Sample streaming frames (conceptual):
- text_delta: {"type":"text_delta","seq":5,"text":"Hello there"}
- partial_json: {"type":"partial_json","schema":"order_v2","path":"/items/0","value":"{"sku": "X-1"}"}
- tool_progress: {"type":"tool_progress","tool":"search","progress":0.43}
- tool_result: {"type":"tool_result","tool":"search","result_ref":"tr_12345","hash":"sha256:...","payload_type":"json","payload":"{...}"}
- commit_marker: {"type":"commit_marker","token":"rt_abc","status":"finalized"}
(above are illustrative; payloads travel as string-encoded JSON frames in the newline-delimited stream)

SDK ergonomics (detailed):
- JavaScript (node & browser): streaming() returns AsyncIterable<Frame>. SDK exposes helpers: frames.on('tool_progress', h), frames.filter('partial_json').map(...). Example usage:

const stream = await client.createStream({prompt, offload_policy: 'defer_fast'});
for await (const frame of stream) {
  if (frame.type === 'text_delta') appendToViewport(frame.text);
  if (frame.type === 'tool_progress') showSpinner(frame.tool, frame.progress);
  if (frame.type === 'tool_result') hydratePlaceholder(frame.result_ref, frame.payload);
}

- Python: async for frame in client.stream(...): same pattern; provide sync wrapper for blocking clients.

- Mobile SDK: prefer minimal callbacks and resumable tokens; avoid long-lived sockets when OS backgrounding is likely. Provide optional server-side webhook to receive tool_result and notify device.

Error and fallback behaviors:
- If a tool call fails and fallback_policy=best-effort: emit tool_result with status:failed and include error_code and optional cached_alternative.
- If fallback_policy=required: stream returns commit_marker with status:failed and the overall call marked failed; clients that require strong guarantees should set this flag.

Observability and Optimize integration:
- Emit token-level attribution: which frames were produced pre- and post-offload.
- Tool traces: latency histogram per tool, percent of offloaded work that returned before stream closed, and failure causes.
- Quality signals: map tool_result hashes to evaluation prompts so Optimize can detect regressions when tool-backed enrichments change.

Rollout plan (phased):
Phase 0 (prototype, internal): build offload pipeline + frame schema, add internal JS client support, test with internal tools (search, DB).
Phase 1 (beta customers): opt-in boolean per project; SDK default returns frames but does not change legacy API shape. Enable webhooks for mobile customers.
Phase 2 (GA): frame schema stable, documented SDK pattern samples, Console shows tool-latency dashboards and per-route offload metrics.

Success metrics:
- p50 initial token token-response latency unchanged for 95% of calls after enabling offload on 50% of beta routes.
- Reduction in user-visible waits for tool-backed augmentations by 60% (because augmentation is delivered asynchronously).
- SDK adoption: 20 beta customers integrate frame handlers in first 3 months.

Operational requirements and limits:
- Offload queue should support configurable per-tenant concurrency limits and safeguards to avoid noisy neighbors.
- Default expiration for offload tasks: 60s; configurable per-route.
- Storage TTL for late-bound results: 24 hours by default, configurable.

Security and compliance:
- All tool_result payloads must be tagged with provenance metadata (requester, timestamp, signed hash if requested).
- For Private deployments: offload pipeline should allow local-only toollets and not export payloads to Redwood-managed queues unless explicitly configured.

Open questions / unresolved tradeoffs:
- Should we support rich binary frames (attachments) in the stream or force payload-by-reference for large results? (Recommendation: reference by default; allow inline small payloads.)
- How to surface ordering semantics when multiple tool results target the same JSON path? We need a deterministic merge policy (latest-wins vs sequence-merge vs user-provided merge handler).
- Billing: how to bill offloaded compute that is delayed or completed after stream close? Propose billing on completion with clear visibility in Console.

Risks and mitigations:
- Complexity for developers: mitigate by shipping SDK helpers and a migration guide with common patterns (placeholders, optimistic UI).
- Operational explosion of background tasks: mitigate with tenant throttles, backpressure, and autoscaling policies for offload workers.
- Data residency concerns for Private deployments: default local-only offload and documented opt-in for cross-region processing.

Migration guidance for customers:
- Minimal-change path: set offload_policy: 'defer_fast' in route config. Client will continue to receive text_delta frames as before. Add optional onFrame('tool_result') handlers to progressively enable enrichment.
- Strong-consistency path: set offload_policy: 'block_required' to retain old behavior; warn about degraded interactive latency.

Implementation sketch (engineering notes):
- Runtime: extend serving runtime to emit preliminary frames as model tokens are produced. Introduce an offload API layer that receives tool invocation intents and returns resume_token.
- Storage: lightweight results store for result_ref -> payload resolution and expiring keys.
- SDKs: frame parsing layer, typed bindings, helper utilities for placeholder management and resume flows.
- Observability: trace IDs join across streaming request, offload job, and any webhook callbacks.

Doc and dev experience deliverables:
- API reference for frame types and route options.
- Migration guide and pattern library (placeholders, optimistic UI, webhook fallback).
- Code samples: JS, Python, mobile pseudo-SDK.

Next steps (action items):
- Product: finalize frame type v1 and fallback policy definitions (owner: Jordan Lee, due 2025-10-10).
- Eng infra: spike on offload queue and storage options (owner: Ethan Morales, due 2025-10-03).
- SDK: implement JS frame API prototype and sample app (owner: Priya Natarajan, due 2025-10-17).
- CS/solutions: identify 3 beta customers and prepare migration playbook (owner: Maya Chen, due 2025-10-20).

Appendix: short example developer story
1) Chat app wants to show quick reply text while also showing fact-checked claim counts from a heavy audit service.
2) Developer uses offload_policy=defer_fast. Client receives text deltas immediately and renders UI; a placeholder widget shows 'loading claims...'.
3) Audit service completes after 1.8s and SDK emits tool_result with payload {claims: 12, sources:[...]} which the app uses to replace the placeholder.

This draft aims to provide a principled, observable, and ergonomic pattern to mix immediate LLM streaming with eventual tool-based enrichment. Feedback welcome on the frame model, fallback semantics, and SDK surfaces we should prioritize for beta.
